title: Drawing Ledger
client: Product for practices that issue drawings
status: Built and tested, first live installation pending
description: Drawing Ledger keeps a drawing transmittal current on Microsoft 365: it reads each PDF's title block, waits for the project lead's yes and never deletes a row.
deck: The drawing fills in the transmittal. The lead still says yes.
summary: A drawing transmittal is a practice's record of what it issued, which revision, to whom and when. Kept by hand, one missed update leaves that record a revision behind.

Drawing Ledger reads each PDF dropped in a project's issue folder, checks the file name against the drawing's own title block, and plans only the difference. The project lead approves from an email. Only then is the client copy replaced, with each drawing number linked to its PDF and old revisions struck through, never deleted.

It runs as one small Azure Functions app with no Power Automate licence, and it signs in to Microsoft Graph with a managed identity, so it stores no password or client secret for Microsoft Graph. It has 290 automated tests. It is built and tested, and the first live installation is pending.

offer.who: Architecture, engineering and construction practices on Microsoft 365 and SharePoint that issue PDF drawings and keep a drawing transmittal in Word.
offer.gets: A transmittal that keeps itself. Each PDF dropped in a project's issue folder becomes a checked row. The project lead approves from an email after a work account sign in. The client copy is replaced with every drawing number linked to its exact PDF, old revisions struck through, deleted files marked Removed, and no row ever deleted. A project list in plain words, a log and a health check come with it.
offer.needs: Microsoft 365 with SharePoint. PDF drawings whose title block prints the drawing number, project code and date as text. A file naming rule with serial, drawing number, project code and revision. A Word transmittal template. A shared mailbox, a small SharePoint site and one approver per project. If your title block or transmittal layout differs from the one it reads today, a small adapter comes first.

Your admin gives about 45 minutes in one sitting for the managed service, or about an hour for your own Azure, then Microsoft's own waits of up to about a day. the-drawing-decides.h2: The drawing decides, not the file name
the-drawing-decides.lede: I took the job apart cell by cell: what each column of a transmittal means, where its value comes from, and which values only a person can decide.
the-drawing-decides.line: File names are typed by people. The title block is what was drawn.
paras: Every value in a row already exists somewhere. The serial, drawing number, project code, revision and title are in the file name someone typed. Most of the same facts, plus the dates, are in the title block someone drew.

So the engine reads both. It takes the drawing number with any sub project prefix, the project code, the first issue date, the revision list when it is printed as text, and the title. When the name and the drawing disagree on number, project or revision, the drawing wins and the file waits for a person.

It asks a person only when there is no single right answer. If a title block draws a revision date as lines instead of text, the lead types it on the approval page. Status starts from the project's default, and the lead can change it per row.
Each check compares the whole issue folder with the transmittal and plans only the difference. A missed or doubled check cannot damage the record, and the same check run twice plans nothing.

every-issue-stays.lede: A transmittal settles an argument only if it still shows what was issued before. So by default the engine adds rows, and it has no way to delete one.
paras: A new revision keeps the old row, strikes it through in red and marks it Revoked, then adds the new row under it. A deleted file keeps its row as well, struck through and marked Removed. A project can choose one row per drawing instead, updated in place, and the first issue date still never changes.

First issued is the drawing's first issue date and never changes. Rev date comes from the title block. The upload date is never used in its place, and impossible dates, such as one before the first issue, are refused.

Each drawing number links to the PDF that row was published from, so an old row points to the old drawing, not the new one. The client copy changes only after the project lead says yes, and only if it is still the version the lead reviewed.
The engine edits the practice's own Word file in place instead of rebuilding it, so the letterhead, the styles and every row it did not touch stay exactly as they were.

the-turn.expected: On Microsoft 365, the obvious build is a Power Automate flow around my code: a trigger, an approval and an email. Azure and Power Automate were both new to me, and three plans broke on Microsoft's own rules while I built.

ruledOut.name: A Power Automate flow calling my code
ruledOut.reason: The free licence limits a flow to standard connectors. Calling my code over HTTP needs a connector outside that set, so the account that owns the flow needs Power Automate Premium.

ruledOut.name: Microsoft's Excel API for the project list
ruledOut.reason: It has no application permission, so an automation identity cannot use it.

ruledOut.name: Sharing links pasted into the project list
ruledOut.reason: Microsoft Graph opens a sharing link for an app only with access to every file in the organisation, which this app must never have.

the-turn.cost: A Power Automate Premium licence for as long as the flow runs, and an identity with far more reach than the job needs.

costMetric.label: per user, paid yearly, plus GST: Microsoft's India list price for Power Automate Premium, read 25 Oct 2026.

the-turn.line: The flow only kept time, asked for a yes and sent mail. A small app could do all three itself.
the-turn.built: One small Azure Functions app with its own timer, its own approval page behind Microsoft sign in, and Microsoft Graph mail. It reads and writes the project list as a whole file, guarded by its version tag, and asks people for the address in the browser bar instead of a sharing link. There is no Power Automate licence to buy, and the app reaches only what it is granted.

five-jobs.lede: An architect's part is two steps: name the PDF by the rule and drop it in the issue folder. Everything after the drop is the engine's job, except one review.
paras: For each drawing issued, the engine does five jobs that are otherwise done by hand [reported:spec]. The project lead keeps one: review and approve, from an email, on a phone or a laptop.

safe-to-leave-running.lede: Software that writes a record people rely on should reach as little as possible, and when something fails it should stop, say so and damage nothing.

paras: It signs in to Microsoft Graph with a managed identity, so it stores no password or client secret for Microsoft Graph. Run as a service across organisations, the app's only credential is that identity, linked by a federated credential.

tiles.label: it can write to, each named by your admin: the site you share with clients and its own small site. Never the main office site, never the whole organisation.
it can send from. A setup step checks that another mailbox is refused.
stored for Microsoft Graph. It signs in with a managed identity.
tiles.note: Two things are stored: one key that signs approval links and seals records, and in a self hosted install, the platform's sign in secret, which expires and has a renewal step.

paras: The approval page sits behind Microsoft sign in. It accepts only an account from the practice's own organisation whose sign in name is the project's approver. The managed service also matches that name to the person's object ID, so a reused or renamed address cannot approve; a self hosted install can switch the same check on.

Links are signed and expire. Opening a link changes nothing, because a mail scanner may open it before anyone reads the email; only the button decides. The page is never cached, cannot be framed by another site and sends a strict content security policy, and its error pages show a short reference, never internals.

Drawings stay in the practice's SharePoint and pass through memory only. Logs hold project codes, file names, statuses and approver addresses, never the text of a document, and the managed service keeps them for 30 days [reported:service].

sections.intro: Every write is checked against the version it read, so it fails rather than overwrite a change it has not seen. The rest is a list of things that will go wrong one day, and what happens then.
rows: A check runs twice, or one is missed
The next check compares the whole folder again. A second run plans nothing.
Someone edits the client copy or replaces a drawing after the lead reviewed it
Publishing stops and a fresh draft goes out. It never overwrites.
The publish lands, then the email fails
The publish stands, because it is recorded the moment the client copy is written. The email goes again at the next check.
Someone edits the record file to approve a change
Its seal breaks. The update is cancelled and reported.
Microsoft asks it to slow down
It waits as asked, up to 60 seconds, for up to 5 attempts [reported:engine]. A write that may have landed is never sent twice.
The transmittal is open in Word, or the project list in Excel
Publishing waits for the next check, and log lines wait in a queue.
One project's folder errors
The other projects still run, and the failed one retries at the next check.
A Word file would come out damaged
It is never saved. A last gate checks every Word file before it is written.
A published transmittal has to be undone
SharePoint's version history restores it, and the next draft starts from the restored version.
sections.after: Checks run every 5 minutes [reported:spec]. When nothing changed, Last checked is stamped at most once an hour, so the project list gains at most one new SharePoint version an hour instead of up to 12 [modelled:engine].

paras: 290 automated tests run with no network, with fakes standing in for Microsoft Graph and Azure. 33 of them came from an adversarial review [measured:tests], and two review rounds fixed over 40 findings [reported:notes].

When I refactored for readability, I checked that the behaviour did not change: 176 output files compared byte for byte, all identical, with no test edited. The longest function went from 86 lines to 44 [measured:optimised].

The same engine runs on a laptop, with plain folders standing in for SharePoint and an outbox folder for mail. There, the end to end rehearsal passed: an approval with a typed date, a revision revoked, a rejection, a removed file, a bad name refused, a rerun that changed nothing, an impersonation refused and hand edits cancelled.
A test also checks the setup guides against the code, so a setting the code needs cannot go missing from a guide.

Nothing has run on a live Microsoft 365 tenant yet. Before the first installation, I listed the Microsoft behaviours the documentation leaves open, each with the check that settles it and a fallback: 19 for the managed service [reported:service] and 15 for a self hosted install [reported:guide].

paras: One Azure Functions app on the Flex Consumption plan, Microsoft Graph and SharePoint. The core uses the Python standard library, and only the title block reader needs an extra package, for PDF text. The runtime needs three packages, each pinned to an exact version, so a deploy or a rollback gets the same versions [measured:engine].

Two hostings come from one zip: I can run it for you as a managed service, or it can be installed in your own Azure on pay as you go. Moving between them is a settings change plus your admin's grants. No data moves, because all state lives in your SharePoint.

3,432 checks × 2 GB × 5 s, an estimate = 34,320 GB seconds
34,320 ÷ 100,000 GB seconds free each month ≈ 0.34, about a third
sections.mathNote: The free grant is 100,000 GB seconds and 250,000 executions a month per subscription, on a paid pay as you go subscription only [reported:functionsprice].
sections.upkeep: Microsoft lists October 2028 as the expected end of support for Python 3.12 on Azure Functions, so the move to a newer runtime is already on my list [reported:functionspython].

sections.h3: What it does not do yet
list: It reads one title block layout and writes one transmittal layout, with one list of status words. A practice with a different layout needs a small adapter, which I have not built yet.
It reads text, not pictures. A scanned or image only PDF is not read.
It has not run on a live Microsoft 365 tenant. A rehearsal on a test tenant comes first, then the first installation.
Two checks from the first review are still open: a warning when a revision jumps, such as R2 to R10, and a check that a revision date is not earlier than the one before.

paras: The rules taught me more than the code did. An API with no application permission, a sharing link that opens only with access to every file, a publish that must be recorded the moment it lands: each one made the design smaller and safer. The lesson I keep is to read the permission table before drawing the architecture.
